KenBench · Phase 1 technical report

How Well Do Open Language Models Handle Kenyan Languages?¶

An evaluation of 12 open language models on 17 benchmarks in Swahili, Dholuo, Kikuyu, Kamba, Luhya, Somali and Oromo, zero-shot and 5-shot

KenyaNLP · KenBench Phase 1 results · lm-evaluation-harness 0.4.9.1 · November 2026

Companion outputs: the interactive explorer (results_report.html) and a code-free version of this analysis (Kenya_NLP_Evaluation_Report.html / .pdf). All three are generated from the same result files.

Abstract¶

We evaluate 12 open language models (125M to 8B parameters) on 17 benchmarks covering seven languages spoken in and around Kenya, zero-shot and with five in-context examples, using lm-evaluation-harness (5,328 task-level scores over 222 task variants). Because the benchmarks differ in metric and number of answer options, every score is rescaled against random guessing and aggregated per benchmark before models are compared. The strongest model, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, reaches 24.3 on this 0–100 above-chance scale with five examples (15.4 zero-shot), far from ceiling. Model size predicts performance (Spearman ρ = 0.77, p = 0.004), while the four Africa-centric models, all under 700M parameters, rank last. Three findings matter for anyone using these benchmarks: 37% of classification runs are degenerate one-label predictions whose raw scores look meaningful; five examples raise scores on most benchmarks but the gain is significant for only 3 of 12 models after correction; and Swahili leads the other Kenyan languages on every benchmark that covers several of them. Kenya-specific tasks remain near the floor (best model, averaged over each benchmark's tasks: KenSwQuAD token F1 22.6, KenPOS accuracy 26.9, MasakhaNER 2.0 span F1 20.4).

Research questions¶

Question Answered in
RQ1 How well do current open language models perform on Kenyan-language tasks, across task types? §4, §5, §6, §14
RQ2 Do five in-context examples help, and where do they hurt? §7, §11
RQ3 How do the Kenyan languages compare with each other on the same task? §8, §9, §12
RQ4 Does model scale or an African-language focus better predict performance? §13
RQ5 How far can the scores be trusted (degenerate predictions, prompt sensitivity, data splits)? §1, §3, §10

Methods in brief¶

  • Models. 12 open checkpoints from 125M to 8B parameters: instruction-tuned decoders (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Phi-3-mini, Aya-23-8B in 4-bit), base decoders (Gemma-2B, GPT-2 Medium/XL, GPT-Neo 125M/2.7B) and four Africa-centric models (InkubaLM-0.4B and the encoder–decoders AfriMT5-base, AfriTeVa-V2-base, Cheetah-base).
  • Benchmarks. 13 AfroBench task families plus 4 custom Kencorpus tasks (KenSwQuAD, KenPOS, KenCorpus genre, MasakhaNER 2.0): 222 task variants once languages, prompt templates and prompting modes (direct, translate-test, chain-of-thought) are expanded.
  • Protocol. EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness 0.4.9.1 on full test sets, zero-shot and 5-shot, greedy decoding. Multiple-choice tasks are scored by option log-likelihood.
  • Metrics. One primary metric per benchmark, following its authors (accuracy, weighted F1, span F1, token F1, exact match or chrF), all on 0–100. To compare benchmarks, each score is rescaled as (score − chance) / (100 − chance) × 100, so 0 is random guessing.
  • Aggregation. Tasks are averaged within each benchmark, then benchmarks with equal weight.
  • Statistics. Stratified bootstrap 95% intervals (2,000 resamples); paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at the benchmark level with Holm correction; one-sided z-tests against chance from harness standard errors; Spearman correlation for scale. One-label runs are detected exactly from the identity weighted F1 = 2p²/(1+p).
  • Data coverage. Every harness result file and every scored cell of the results-tracker workbooks, including results run by partner teams, was read and matched to the main grid (Appendix A; Data coverage tab). Rankings and tests use the complete 12-model × 17-benchmark grid of KenBench harness runs. Partner-team results for other models (Phi-3-mini-128k, Llama-3-8B, GPT-2) and benchmarks (MASSIVE, AfriHate, AfriDOC-MT, FLORES English→Swahili) are scored with the same rules and shown with all other results; because they cover fewer models or benchmarks, they do not enter the overall rank, which averages the 17 benchmarks shared by the fully-tested models. Partner-team runs that overlap ours serve as a replication check; where values differ, the harness value is used. 2-example smoke tests are excluded.

2. Metrics, primary-metric choice and chance levels¶

Each benchmark family emits several metrics. One primary metric is used throughout, matching how the benchmark's authors report it:

  • Accuracy for balanced multiple-choice tasks (AfriXNLI, Belebele, AfriMMLU).
  • Weighted F1 for classification with imbalanced classes (AfriSenti, MasakhaNEWS, Injongo, SIB-200, KenCorpus). Accuracy is kept as a secondary metric.
  • Span F1 (NER), token accuracy (POS), token F1 (extractive/open QA), exact match (math) for generative tasks.
  • chrF for translation. BLEU is secondary because it is below 5 for most models here and does not separate them.

All scores are put on a 0–100 scale. Because a raw 33 means random guessing on a 3-class task but a strong result on a 40-class task, cross-benchmark aggregates use the above-chance score:

$$\text{above-chance} = \frac{\text{score} - \text{chance}}{100 - \text{chance}} \times 100, \qquad \text{chance} = 100 / k$$

where $k$ is the number of answer options (0 for generative tasks). For weighted F1 the uniform-guess baseline is exactly $100/k$ only for balanced classes, so on skewed sets (AfriSenti, KenCorpus) it is an approximation.

Table 1b. Metric glossary.

Name Range Definition Caveat
Accuracy 0-100 Share of examples where the model's answer is the gold answer. For multiple-choice tasks the harness scores each option by log-likelihood and picks the most likely one. On imbalanced data a model that always picks the largest class can look good.
Weighted F1 0-100 F1 (harmonic mean of precision and recall) per class, averaged with weights equal to each class's share of the test set (scikit-learn average='weighted'). A model that predicts one class for everything scores 2p²/(1+p), where p is that class's share; this identity is used to flag one-label runs. The chance level 100/k used for above-chance scores is exact only for balanced classes; on skewed data (AfriSenti, KenCorpus) random guessing scores lower, so modest negative values are possible.
Span F1 0-100 For NER: precision and recall over predicted entity spans. A span counts only if its text and entity type both match. Depends on the model producing the expected output format; formatting errors score 0.
Token accuracy 0-100 For POS tagging: share of words whose generated tag equals the gold tag. Sensitive to output-format errors such as missing or extra tags.
Exact match 0-100 Share of examples where the extracted answer string equals the gold answer after light normalisation (whitespace, case, punctuation). Very strict; small surface differences score 0.
Token F1 0-100 SQuAD-style overlap of words between generated and gold answer. Gives partial credit, so it is always ≥ exact match.
chrF 0-100 Character n-gram F-score between translation and reference (sacreBLEU). Works better than BLEU for morphologically rich languages. Not comparable across language pairs with different scripts or morphology.
BLEU 0-100 Word n-gram precision with a brevity penalty (sacreBLEU). Shown as a secondary metric. Very low (under 5) for most models here, so chrF separates them better.
Above-chance score ≤100 (score − chance) / (100 − chance) × 100. 0 means random guessing, 100 means perfect. Puts tasks with 3, 7 or 40 classes on one footing. For generative tasks chance is 0, so it equals the raw score. Negative values mean worse than random guessing.
Standard error Harness bootstrap / binomial standard error of a task score. ±1.96 × SE gives an approximate 95% confidence interval. Not reported for NER, POS or KenPOS.

3. Data quality¶

3.1 One-label (constant) predictors¶

If a classifier outputs the same label for every input, its accuracy equals that label's share $p$ and its weighted F1 is exactly

$$F1_w = p \cdot \frac{2p}{1+p} = \frac{2p^2}{1+p}.$$

Runs matching this identity to within 0.01 points are flagged constant_pred. Their scores reflect the label distribution of the test set, not language understanding. The gap distribution below is sharply bimodal (an exact cluster at 0), so the threshold is not sensitive.

Figure 1. Distance of each classification run from the one-label identity (log scale). Runs left of the line predict a single label for every input. Table 3. Share of one-label runs per model and benchmark.

Reading: the three encoder–decoder models (AfriMT5, AfriTeVa-V2, Cheetah) are pretrained-only span-corruption models. Scored by log-likelihood over label strings, they almost always prefer the same label regardless of input, so their classification scores carry no signal. KenCorpus is the most affected benchmark for every model: its genre distribution is very skewed (e.g. ~96% of the Luo test set is one genre), so a one-label model reaches high accuracy and high weighted F1.

4. Overall leaderboard¶

The aggregate is a macro-average. Scores are first averaged over the task variants (prompts, modes, languages) within each benchmark, then over the 17 benchmarks with equal weight, on the above-chance scale. The 95% intervals come from a stratified bootstrap that resamples tasks within each benchmark (2,000 replicates). The mean rank (1 = best on a benchmark) is a scale-free check on the ordering.

6. Are the top models significantly different?¶

Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on the 17 benchmark-level above-chance means (few-shot), Holm-corrected across all pairs. Benchmarks are the unit of replication, so the test asks whether one model is consistently better across benchmarks rather than on many prompts of the same benchmark.

7. Few-shot effect¶

For each model the zero-shot to few-shot change is averaged over the task variants of each benchmark, and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test is run over the 17 benchmark means, Holm-corrected over the 12 models. Testing at the benchmark level matters: the five prompt templates of one task are not independent, and treating all 222 task variants as separate observations would overstate significance. Task-level win and tie rates are shown for description only.

Reading: few-shot beats zero-shot on at least 70% of benchmarks for 9 of 12 models, but after correction the gain is significant only for Gemma-2B, GPT-Neo-2.7B and GPT-Neo-125M, because it is concentrated in a few benchmarks. Five examples help most strongly on topic and intent classification (MasakhaNEWS, SIB-200, Injongo) and on AfriQA. The largest regressions are on generative, format-sensitive tasks: MasakhaPOS drops 16–30 points for all four strongest models, and AfriMGSM drops about 10 points for Llama-3.2-3B and Phi-3-mini. KenCorpus drops for the small base models. The likely mechanism is that the examples change the output format the model produces. Note also that the KenCorpus "drop" for GPT-2 / GPT-Neo is partly a move away from a one-label prediction that happened to match the majority genre.

8. Languages¶

Language comparisons are only valid within one benchmark, because each language is covered by a different mix of tasks. For example, Kamba and Kikuyu appear only in SIB-200 and FLORES, while Swahili appears in all 17. Pooling across benchmarks mostly measures which benchmarks a language happens to have.

Figure 11. Model size vs overall score. Larger markers are Africa-centric models.

Africa-centric median -1.4 vs general 11.6; one-sided Mann-Whitney U = 0, p = 0.002 (n = 4 vs 8)

Reading: size is the strongest single predictor of score. The comparison is confounded, though: every Africa-centric model here is small (≤ 664M) and three of the four are pretrained-only encoder–decoders that are poorly suited to prompted evaluation. So this result shows that these Africa-centric checkpoints do not compete under prompting. It does not show that African-language pretraining fails. InkubaLM-0.4B, the only Africa-centric decoder, is the fairest comparison and still sits near the bottom.

15. Conclusions¶

Answers to the research questions, computed from the data. The same text appears on the Report tab of the web explorer.

RQ1: How well do open language models perform on Kenyan-language tasks? Poorly overall, with a few bright spots. The best model, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, reaches 24.3 on the above-chance scale with five examples. Only Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B and Phi-3-mini are significantly above chance on at least a quarter of the balanced multiple-choice tasks. News-topic classification and Swahili open QA are the bright spots (best MasakhaNEWS weighted F1 60.6, AfriQA token F1 62.9); tagging, maths and the Kenya-specific tasks stay near the floor.

RQ2: Do five in-context examples help, and where do they hurt? Usually, but unevenly; they hurt structured-output tasks. 9 of 12 models score higher on at least 70% of benchmarks with five examples, but the gain is significant at the benchmark level for only 3 (Gemma-2B, GPT-Neo-2.7B and GPT-Neo-125M). Examples hurt format-sensitive generation: MasakhaPOS drops 16–29 points for the four strongest models, and AfriMGSM drops 9–10 points for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Phi-3-mini.

RQ3: How do the Kenyan languages compare on the same task? Swahili leads everywhere; Luo, Kikuyu and Kamba trail far behind. On SIB-200 the four strongest models score 41–74 weighted F1 in Swahili but 29–47 in the other languages. FLORES translation into English peaks at 28.8 chrF from Swahili against 17.8–20.4 from the others. English→Luo is the hardest direction (13.7 chrF vs 43.7 for English→Swahili).

RQ4: Does model scale or an African-language focus better predict performance? Scale, though the comparison is confounded. Size and overall score correlate strongly (Spearman ρ = 0.77, p = 0.004). The Africa-centric models rank 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 12, but they are also the smallest and three are pretrained-only encoder–decoders, so this is not a verdict on African-language pretraining.

RQ5: How far can the scores be trusted? With care: many runs are degenerate and prompts matter. 37% of classification runs predict one label for every input. Prompt wording alone moves scores by a median of 7.9 points on AfriSenti and 5.7 on MasakhaNEWS. 6 benchmarks draw few-shot examples from the split they are scored on. KenPOS test sets have as few as 9 sentences.

Headline findings (as shown on the explorer's Findings tab):

  1. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct leads overall. Averaged over all 17 benchmarks on the above-chance scale, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct scores 24.3 with 5 examples and 15.4 zero-shot. Even the best model is far from ceiling: most Kenyan-language tasks remain hard.
  2. Five examples usually help, but unevenly. With five in-context examples, 9 of 12 models score higher on at least 70% of the 17 benchmarks. Largest mean gains: Gemma-2B +11.2, Phi-3-mini +8.8, Aya-23-8B +7.9 points. Tested at the benchmark level (paired Wilcoxon, n = 17, Holm-corrected over 12 models), the gain is significant for 3 models (Gemma-2B, GPT-Neo-2.7B, GPT-Neo-125M); for the rest it is too uneven across benchmarks. The largest drop is Phi-3-mini on MasakhaPOS (−29.5 points), likely because the examples change the output format the model produces.
  3. Many classification runs predict one label. 37% of classification runs give the same label for every input (detected exactly from accuracy vs weighted F1). The three seq2seq models (AfriMT5-base, Cheetah-base, AfriTeVa-V2-base) do this in 91% of runs. Their scores reflect label frequencies, not understanding; they are pretrained-only and not built for prompting.
  4. Scale matters more than African-language focus. Model size and overall few-shot score correlate strongly (Spearman ρ = 0.77, p = 0.004, n = 12). The Africa-centric models are all under 700M parameters and sit at the bottom: InkubaLM-0.4B reaches 2.8 few-shot, below GPT-2 XL.
  5. Swahili is far ahead of other Kenyan languages. Where the same task covers several languages, Swahili leads: best FLORES chrF into English is 28.8 for Swahili vs 17.8 (Luo), 20.4 (Kikuyu) and 17.9 (Kamba). On MAFAND, English→Luo peaks at 13.7 chrF against 43.7 for English→Swahili. Compare languages only within one benchmark: each language is covered by a different set of tasks.
  6. Kenya-specific tasks are close to the floor. Best few-shot scores (best model, averaged over each benchmark's tasks): KenSwQuAD token F1 22.6, KenPOS accuracy 26.9, MasakhaNER 2.0 span F1 20.4. Zero-shot KenPOS is near 0 for every model, so these models cannot tag Dholuo or Luhya without examples.
  7. Prompt wording moves scores by several points. For the same model, language and setting, the gap between the best and worst of the five prompt templates has a median of 7.9 points on AfriSenti and 5.7 on MasakhaNEWS. Single-prompt comparisons between close models are unreliable; the report averages over prompts.

Limitations¶

  • Prompted log-likelihood evaluation does not suit the pretrained-only encoder–decoders (AfriMT5, AfriTeVa-V2, Cheetah); their low scores reflect the protocol, not their potential after fine-tuning.
  • Aya-23-8B ran in 4-bit, which may cost a few points relative to full precision.
  • Chance level for weighted F1 assumes balanced classes; on skewed sets the true random baseline is lower.
  • Six benchmarks draw few-shot examples from the split they are scored on, and the Kencorpus tasks are scored on the train split, so few-shot gains there may be slightly optimistic.
  • KenPOS and KenCorpus-Luo have small test sets, and KenCorpus is dominated by one genre.
  • Languages are covered by different benchmarks, so pooled language averages are confounded; compare languages within one benchmark.
  • One run per model and setting with greedy decoding; spread across prompt templates is the only measure of run-to-run variation.
  • The model set has no current frontier or closed models, so it shows where open small models stand rather than the state of the art.

Reproducibility statement¶

All scores come from the per-model CSVs and harness JSON files in nlp_evals/. Every table, figure and finding in this notebook, the web explorer and the code-free report is regenerated by Restart & Run All. Run commands, seeds, batch sizes, dataset sources and splits are listed in §1 and on the About & reproduce tab of the explorer.

Cite the underlying benchmarks (sources in Table 1) and the harness. For these results:

Appendix A. Data coverage and supplementary results¶

This appendix shows that no result was left out. It reads every harness result file on disk (main runs, the 4-bit test run and the smoke tests) and every scored cell of the Dataset_Specific_Results_Tracker*.xlsx workbooks, then matches each one against the main grid (results_inventory.py).

  • Main grid: the complete 12-model × 17-benchmark × 2-setting grid. Every ranking, figure and test in §1–§15 uses only this grid, so that all models are compared on identical tasks.
  • Partner-team results: results run by partner teams and transferred to the tracker. Runs of models or benchmarks outside the grid are scored with the same rules (Table A6) and shown in the web explorer marked team, without an overall rank. Runs that overlap ours are used as a replication check (Table A7).
  • Other separate results: our 4-bit AfriTeVa-V2 test run, kept out of the grid because the full-precision run is used.
  • Excluded: smoke tests run on 2 examples per task to check the pipeline. Their scores carry no information.
  • Tracker cells either repeat a harness value or differ from it (older runs, manual entry). When they differ, the harness value is used.

419 harness result files were read: 409 for the main grid (5,328 task runs = 12 models × 222 task variants × 2 settings), one 4-bit test (10 task runs) and smoke tests (32 task runs). All 10,032 metric values in the per-model CSVs match their JSON files exactly. 20,984 tracker cells were checked.

Reading: nothing on disk is missing from the report. Partner-team results fill gaps the main grid does not cover: a 128k-context Phi-3-mini (close to the 4k model on most classification benchmarks, higher on MasakhaNER), Llama-3-8B and GPT-2 on MASSIVE, and Gemma-2B on MASSIVE, AfriHate, AfriDOC-MT and English→Swahili FLORES. Because they cover different subsets, they are shown alongside the grid rather than ranked within it. Where partner teams ran the same configuration as us, most values agree exactly, as expected from deterministic greedy evaluation; the largest gaps are in MasakhaPOS (109 placeholder values of 1.0), MasakhaNEWS and MasakhaNER 2.0 (median gaps of about 28 and 15 points among differing values), which point to different harness versions or transcription rather than model behaviour. AfriHate's 5-shot accuracy of 1.0 in both languages is implausible and should be re-checked before it is cited. The 4-bit AfriTeVa-V2 run matches the full-precision run exactly, because both predict one label.
